questions.question: What does the pwd command do and when would you use it?
questions.answer: pwd (Print Working Directory) displays the full absolute path of your current location in the Linux filesystem. You use it whenever you need to confirm where you are — especially after navigating through multiple directories or when writing scripts that depend on the current location.

questions.question: What is the difference between ls, ls -a, ls -l, and ls -la?
questions.answer: ls lists visible files and directories. ls -a shows all files including hidden ones (starting with dot). ls -l shows long format with permissions, owner, size, and timestamps. ls -la combines both — long format for all files including hidden. Use ls -la when you want the most complete picture of a directory.

questions.question: How do you identify a hidden file in Linux?
questions.answer: Any file or directory whose name starts with a dot (.) is hidden in Linux. For example: .ssh, .bashrc, .bash_history. They are not shown by the default ls command. Use ls -a to reveal them.

questions.question: What is the difference between an absolute path and a relative path?
questions.answer: An absolute path starts from root (/) and is the full path regardless of your current location — like /home/ec2-user/projects. A relative path is based on your current directory and does not start with / — like projects/2025 (only valid if you're already in /home/ec2-user).

questions.question: What does mkdir -p do and why is the -p flag important?
questions.answer: mkdir -p creates nested directory structures in a single command. Without -p, mkdir fails if parent directories don't exist. With -p, it creates all missing parent directories in the path. It's also idempotent — running it again on an existing path produces no error.

questions.question: What is the difference between rmdir and rm -r?
questions.answer: rmdir only removes empty directories — it fails with an error if the directory contains any files or subdirectories. rm -r recursively removes a directory and all its contents. Use rmdir for safe cleanup of empty folders, and rm -r when you want to delete everything inside as well.

questions.question: What happens when you run rm on a file in Linux? Is there any way to recover it?
questions.answer: rm permanently deletes the file with no Recycle Bin, no Trash, and no undo. Recovery is not possible through normal means once rm is run. In an AWS environment, you might recover from a snapshot or backup (EBS snapshots, S3 versioning), but the file itself is gone from the filesystem.

questions.question: What is the .ssh directory on EC2 and what is inside it?
questions.answer: The .ssh directory at /home/ec2-user/.ssh contains SSH authentication files. The most important is authorized_keys, which holds the public keys allowed to SSH into this user account. AWS automatically places your public key there when you launch an EC2 instance with a key pair.

questions.question: What does the history command do and where is history stored?
questions.answer: The history command lists all previously typed commands, numbered in order. History is stored in ~/.bash_history (in your home directory) and persists across terminal sessions. You can re-run command number N using !N, or re-run the last command using !!.

questions.question: What does the $ versus # symbol at the end of the Linux prompt indicate?
questions.answer: $ indicates you are logged in as a regular non-root user. # indicates you are logged in as root (the superuser). On EC2, you connect as ec2-user which shows $. If you switch to root (sudo su), the prompt changes to #. This is a quick visual indicator of your privilege level.

questions.question: Describe a situation where a student on EC2 cannot connect after creating an instance. What are the first things you would check?
questions.answer: (Situation) A student gets a connection refused error SSHing to EC2. (Task) Diagnose and resolve within the session. (Action) First check: Is the instance in Running state? Check the security group inbound rules — port 22 must be open. Verify they're using the correct username (ec2-user for Amazon Linux). Confirm they're using the right key pair file and the correct public IP. Check if they have the .pem file and its permissions are 400. (Result) Most EC2 SSH issues trace back to one of these five areas.

questions.question: A student ran rmdir on a directory and got 'Directory not empty'. Walk through your diagnostic and resolution.
questions.answer: (Situation) rmdir fails with 'Directory not empty' error. (Task) Help the student delete the directory. (Action) First, cd into the directory and run ls -la to see what's inside — there are files or subdirectories present. Explain that rmdir only works on truly empty directories. If they want to delete everything inside too, use rm -r foldername. If they want to keep the contents and only remove the directory shell, move the files first. (Result) rm -r resolves the issue immediately.

questions.question: A classmate on Windows cannot connect to EC2 using PuTTY despite having the key file. What's the likely issue?
questions.answer: (Situation) PuTTY connection fails even with the key file provided. (Task) Identify the format mismatch. (Action) AWS provides keys in .pem format. PuTTY requires .ppk format. The student must open PuTTYgen, load the .pem file, and save it as .ppk. Then load the .ppk file in PuTTY under Connection > SSH > Auth > Credentials. Also check that the username is ec2-user, not root or ubuntu. (Result) Converting the key format with PuTTYgen resolves the authentication failure.

questions.question: You're writing a bash script that creates a project folder structure. Why would you use mkdir -p instead of mkdir?
questions.answer: (Situation) Script needs to set up a directory tree. (Task) Choose the right mkdir command for reliability. (Action) Use mkdir -p because: 1) It creates all parent directories if they don't exist. 2) It doesn't fail if the directory already exists — making the script safe to run multiple times (idempotent). mkdir without -p would crash the script if any parent is missing or if you run it twice. (Result) mkdir -p makes scripts reliable and rerunnable.

questions.question: You navigated five levels deep in the filesystem and need to get back to your home directory quickly. What are your options?
questions.answer: (Situation) You're deep in the directory tree. (Task) Return to home as fast as possible. (Action) Three equivalent options: 1) cd with no arguments. 2) cd ~ (tilde shortcut). 3) cd /home/ec2-user (absolute path). All three go to your home directory regardless of where you are. You can also use cd - to go back to the previous directory if needed. (Result) cd ~ is the fastest and most portable.

questions.question: A student deleted a critical configuration file with rm and it's gone. How do you respond?
questions.answer: (Situation) rm permanently deleted an important file on EC2. (Task) Assess recovery options. (Action) In plain Linux, rm is final — no trash. Recovery options: 1) If the EC2 instance has EBS snapshots, restore from the most recent one. 2) If the file was in S3 and versioning was enabled, restore from S3. 3) If it was a config file, recreate it manually from documentation. (Result) Emphasize that rm has no undo — best practice is to back up critical files before deletion and use rm -i for interactive confirmation.

questions.question: You run ls -l and see a line starting with 'd'. What does that tell you, and what would you do next to explore it?
questions.answer: (Situation) ls -l shows a line starting with d. (Task) Understand and explore it. (Action) The 'd' at the start means it's a directory (not a file). To explore it: use cd directoryname to navigate into it, then ls -la to see its contents including hidden files. Use pwd to confirm your location inside it. (Result) The first character of ls -l output — d, -, l — always tells you the type of the filesystem object.

questions.question: How would you create the following structure in one bash session: webapp/src/components, webapp/src/utils, webapp/tests?
questions.answer: (Situation) Need to create a specific multi-branch directory tree. (Task) Build it efficiently using CLI. (Action) Use mkdir -p for each branch: mkdir -p webapp/src/components then mkdir -p webapp/src/utils then mkdir -p webapp/tests. Since -p is idempotent, running these won't fail even if webapp or src already exist from a previous command. Verify with ls -R webapp. (Result) Three mkdir -p commands build the full structure.

questions.question: What is authorized_keys and how does SSH key authentication work on EC2?
questions.answer: authorized_keys is a file at /home/ec2-user/.ssh/authorized_keys that stores public keys. When you SSH in, your SSH client presents your private key. The EC2 instance checks if the matching public key is in authorized_keys. If it matches, access is granted — no password needed. AWS places your public key here automatically when you select a key pair during instance launch. You never send your private key to the server.

questions.question: A student asks: can I recover my EC2 instance if I lose the private key? What do you tell them?
questions.answer: (Situation) Student has lost their .pem file. (Task) Assess and advise. (Action) AWS does not store private keys — this is by design. The private key is downloaded once at creation. Options: 1) If the instance data is not critical, terminate and launch a new instance with a new key pair. 2) If the data matters, the EBS volume can be detached from the broken instance and reattached to a new instance as a secondary volume — then access the data from the new instance. (Result) Always back up private keys securely. There is no 'forgot my key' button on AWS.

questions.question: How would you use Linux CLI commands to audit what commands were run on an EC2 instance during a security incident?
questions.answer: The primary tool is the history command which reads ~/.bash_history. Run history to see all recorded commands for the current user. Also check /var/log/auth.log (or /var/log/secure on Amazon Linux) for SSH login events. The history file can be viewed directly with cat ~/.bash_history. Note that history can be cleared with history -c or by deleting .bash_history — so for forensic purposes, also check OS-level audit logs (auditd) and CloudTrail for API activity.

questions.question: Explain how the Linux filesystem hierarchy relates to AWS EC2 storage architecture.
questions.answer: Linux mounts the root filesystem (/) on the primary EBS volume (usually /dev/xvda). Additional EBS volumes appear as separate block devices and must be mounted to a directory (mount point) in the tree. For example, a data volume mounted at /data becomes accessible via standard Linux paths. EFS (Elastic File System) can be mounted at a path like /mnt/efs. Instance Store volumes are ephemeral — deleted when the instance stops. Understanding the filesystem hierarchy helps you know where data lives and how it's backed up.

questions.question: What are the security implications of file permissions shown in ls -l output for the .ssh directory?
questions.answer: The .ssh directory should have permissions 700 (drwx------) — only the owner can read, write, and execute. authorized_keys should be 600 (-rw-------) — only the owner can read and write. If permissions are too open (e.g., 777), SSH will refuse to connect for security reasons. This is why when you set up SSH keys manually, you run chmod 700 ~/.ssh and chmod 600 ~/.ssh/authorized_keys. AWS handles this automatically for EC2 key pairs.

questions.question: How would you use cat, mkdir, and file redirection together to automate creating a configuration file?
questions.answer: You can combine commands using shell redirection. Example: mkdir -p /home/ec2-user/app/config creates the directory tree. Then cat > /home/ec2-user/app/config/settings.txt followed by typing content and Ctrl+D creates a file with that content. Or: echo '[database]' > config.ini && echo 'host=localhost' >> config.ini chains file creation. This is the basis of shell scripting — combining basic CLI commands with redirection operators (>, >>) to build automation workflows.

questions.question: How does understanding Linux CLI basics help you work more effectively with AWS services beyond EC2?
questions.answer: Linux CLI is the foundation for nearly all AWS engineering work. Elastic Beanstalk, ECS, Lambda (container-based), CodeDeploy, and Systems Manager all interact with Linux environments. S3 is accessed via the AWS CLI which runs in your Linux terminal. CloudFormation and Terraform are run from CLI. CI/CD pipelines (CodePipeline, Jenkins, GitHub Actions) execute shell commands. Understanding pwd, ls, cd, mkdir, rm, cat, and history makes you effective not just on EC2, but across the entire AWS ecosystem where automation and scripting are central.
